title: God our mother
hookLine: Julian of Norwich wrote of Jesus as our true mother

cards: A woman lies so sick that the people around her expect her to die. A priest holds a crucifix before her face. Then, as she later wrote, she was given a series of showings: visions of Christ and his love.

She recovered, kept thinking about what she had seen, and wrote it down. You met her in years one and three: Julian of Norwich, a woman who lived a life of prayer beside a church in that English city.
Among the things she wrote is this: Jesus is our mother.

teach.h: FATHER AND MOTHER, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Julian wasn't throwing out the old words. She calls God our Father, plainly and often. But she sets the two side by side: as truly as God is our Father, God is our Mother.
And she gives the motherhood above all to Jesus. Why Jesus? Look at what a mother does.

teach.h: BIRTH, FOOD, AND A HAND UP.
teach.b: She carries a child in her own body and brings it into life through pain; Julian looks at the cross and sees Christ laboring to bring us to birth.
A mother feeds her child from herself; Julian sees Christ feeding his people with himself in the sacrament. A mother doesn't stop loving a child who falls in the mud; she picks it up and washes it.
Julian says Christ does the same when we fail, without contempt. She didn't invent the picture out of nothing. Scripture already holds it.

teach.h: AS ONE WHOM HIS MOTHER COMFORTETH.
teach.b: In Isaiah, God says, "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you."
And earlier: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee."

teach.h: AS A HEN GATHERETH HER CHICKENS.
teach.b: Jesus himself, grieving over Jerusalem, says, "how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings." Julian wove a picture like this into a whole way of seeing.
Christians use her picture in different ways. Some pray with her words. Others keep to the Father language of the creeds and the Lord's Prayer while still honoring her.
Julian herself held both, and saw no contest between them.

how: Some Christians pray with Julian of Norwich's words and read her Revelations of Divine Love; churches keep the Father language of the creeds and the Lord's Prayer, and some also use scripture's mother images for God's care, as in Isaiah 66:13.

a prayer Julian wrote for her own mother's healing
Julian's picture of Christ's care, beside God as Father

Isaiah: "as one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you."
Jesus compared himself to a hen gathering her chickens
Matthew 23:37: "even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."

games.q: you're Julian. on your sickbed you've seen Christ's love, and now you're searching for words for it. which picture do you reach for?
o: a judge reading out a sentence.
a mother who births, feeds, and picks up her child.
a king far away on a throne.
games.why: Julian calls Jesus our true mother: laboring on the cross, feeding his people, lifting them when they fall. and she still calls God Father.

practice: Bring to mind one picture of that kind of care: a cool hand on a feverish forehead, a child lifted up after a fall, someone awake in the night with a crying baby.
If your own story with a mother is hard, choose a different picture; anyone who has cared like that will do. Let it stay a while, and if you pray, hold it up to God the way Julian did.

wordCard.voice: God our mother. Julian of Norwich's picture of Christ who births, feeds and lifts us up, as truly as God is our Father.

orig.note: Hebrew, mother. In Isaiah 66:13 God's comfort is pictured as a mother's.

carryVoice: Your line: our true mother. Care that picks you up without contempt. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 3 (the sickbed) and ch. 58–61 (Christ our mother)
